## The Setup

Working in restaurants, I heard a recurring theme from the men around me:

> *"Don't get married, kid. Biggest mistake of my life."*

This came up constantly—from customers, from coworkers, from managers. And plenty of other older men throughout my life... The narrative was clear: **marriage ruins your financial life.**

But is this actually true? Does the data support it?

---

## The Question

**Do married men actually earn less than never-married men?**

I analyzed 1994 U.S. Census data to investigate whether marriage is truly a "financial penalty" or just a story men tell themselves.

---

## The Data

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

data <- read.csv("adult.data", header = FALSE, strip.white = TRUE)

colnames(data) <- c("age", "workclass", "fnlwgt", "education", "education.num", 
                    "marital.status", "occupation", "relationship", "race", "sex", 
                    "capital.gain", "capital.loss", "hours.per.week", "native.country", "income")

data_male <- data[data$sex == "Male", ]
data_male <- data_male[data_male$marital.status != "?", ]
data_male <- data_male[data_male$education != "?", ]
data_male$income_binary <- ifelse(data_male$income == ">50K", 1, 0)

cat("Total male observations:", nrow(data_male), "\n")
cat("\nMarital status breakdown:\n")
print(table(data_male$marital.status))
```

---

## The Heatmap: Marriage & Income by Education

```{r}
#| label: heatmap-viz
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6

main_statuses <- c("Married-civ-spouse", "Never-married", "Divorced")

education_order <- c("Preschool", "1st-4th", "5th-6th", "7th-8th", "9th", "10th", "11th", "12th", 
                     "HS-grad", "Some-college", "Assoc-voc", "Assoc-acdm", "Bachelors", 
                     "Masters", "Prof-school", "Doctorate")

heatmap_data <- data_male %>%
  filter(marital.status %in% main_statuses) %>%
  filter(education %in% education_order) %>%
  group_by(marital.status, education) %>%
  summarize(pct_over_50k = mean(income_binary) * 100, count = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(education = factor(education, levels = education_order),
         marital.status = factor(marital.status, levels = main_statuses))

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = education, y = marital.status, fill = pct_over_50k)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct_over_50k, 1), "%")),
            color = "white", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#d73027", high = "#1a9850",
                      name = "% Earning\n>$50K", limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Income Disparity by Marriage Status & Education",
       subtitle = "Percentage of men earning >$50K annually (1994 Census Data)",
       x = "Education Level", y = "Marital Status",
       caption = "Data source: UCI Adult Census Income Dataset") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 10),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "right",
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

---

## Key Statistics

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false

married_pct <- mean(data_male[data_male$marital.status == "Married-civ-spouse", ]$income_binary) * 100
never_married_pct <- mean(data_male[data_male$marital.status == "Never-married", ]$income_binary) * 100
divorced_pct <- mean(data_male[data_male$marital.status == "Divorced", ]$income_binary) * 100

cat("Married men earning >$50K:      ", round(married_pct, 1), "%\n")
cat("Never-married men earning >$50K:", round(never_married_pct, 1), "%\n")
cat("Divorced men earning >$50K:     ", round(divorced_pct, 1), "%\n\n")

contingency <- table(data_male$marital.status, data_male$income)
chi_test <- chisq.test(contingency)
cat("Chi-square p-value:", format(chi_test$p.value, scientific = TRUE), "\n")
cat("Result: HIGHLY SIGNIFICANT (p < 0.001)\n\n")

married_hours <- mean(data_male[data_male$marital.status == "Married-civ-spouse", ]$hours.per.week)
never_married_hours <- mean(data_male[data_male$marital.status == "Never-married", ]$hours.per.week)

cat("Married men avg hours/week:      ", round(married_hours, 1), "\n")
cat("Never-married men avg hours/week:", round(never_married_hours, 1), "\n")
```

---

## What the Heatmap Reveals

- **The opposite of the narrative**: Married men actually earn MORE than never-married men across almost every education level.

- **Education is the real divider**: A Doctorate or Masters degree dramatically increases earning potential regardless of marital status.

- **The married advantage**: At the bachelor's level, married men have a substantial income edge over never-married men.

- **Selection effects**: Older, more established men are more likely to be married AND earn more.

---

## The Conclusion

**The men at the restaurant were wrong — or at least, misleading.**

The data shows:

- ✅ Married men earn MORE, not less
- ✅ The "marriage penalty" is a myth
- ✅ What REALLY matters is education and job choice

The actual story: these men felt constrained by family responsibilities and financial pressure. But that's not a marriage penalty — that's life stage and occupation.
